author: Ahmed Ibrahim
title: Nisman Case: New Evidence & Political Implications
text:
Argentina Reopens Nisman Death Investigation Amidst Political Turmoil A decade-old case, long used as a political weapon, resurfaces as new charges are leveled against former prosecutors and judges, fueling accusations of politically motivated investigations.
The death of Argentine prosecutor Alberto Nisman in 2015 continues to reverberate through the nation’s political landscape, resurfacing once again as a focal point amidst current controversies surrounding recently revealed audio recordings involving Diego Spagnuolo. On Thursday, former Fiscal Viviana Fein and Judge Manuel de Campos were formally charged with alleged irregularities in the handling of the crime scene following Nisman’s death on January 18, 2015 – almost eleven years ago. The timing of the charges has ignited accusations of a politically motivated attempt to deflect attention from the Spagnuolo audios.
The investigation, led by prosecutor Eduardo Taiano, has struggled to gain traction in establishing a theory of murder, despite widespread speculation about a coordinated attack. Popular theories, often parodied, have pointed fingers at a complex network – “A Venezuelan-Iran-Mapuche-Kirchnerist command,” as one satirical take put it. However, investigators have been unable to determine how anyone could have entered Nisman’s secured apartment, or the locked bathroom where he was found. Lacking concrete evidence, Taiano has focused on peripheral issues, such as the actions of law enforcement that night and communications records from the former intelligence agency, SIDE. Critics argue these efforts are a distraction, consistently emerging when the current administration, led by President Javier Milei, faces difficulties.
Detailed accounts from the initial investigation reveal a meticulous, by-the-book approach to securing the scene. Nicolás Vega Laiún, the Federal Police principal at the time, outlined the procedures followed, emphasizing the importance of minimizing contamination. Criminalist Raúl Torre noted that “there is no immaculate scene from the moment one or more doctors enter to see whether or not the person is alive.” Prosecutor Fein, recognizing this, ordered the scene to be filmed from the outside before anyone entered, followed by photographic documentation. Ballistics experts then secured the weapon, identified it, and prepared for potential evidence collection. A forensic doctor, Gabriela Piroso, analyzed the body for injuries and estimated the time of death. The process continued with chemical testing to determine if Nisman had discharged the firearm, followed by fingerprint analysis. The meticulous process, adhering to international standards, involved both gloved and ungloved procedures to preserve evidence.
A Federal Police report from January 26, 2015, spanning 842 pages, details the search for fingerprints belonging to Nisman, his mother Sara Garfunkel, computer scientist Diego Lagomarsino, and domestic employee Gladys Gallardo. While 11 partial prints were recovered, none could be definitively identified. Footprints belonging to Nisman were found on a service door and a nearby cell phone. Importantly, the investigation found no signs of a struggle within the apartment, and a review of 80 out of 101 security cameras revealed no unauthorized entry.
According to reports from Clarín newspaper, the charges against Fein and Campos center on allegations that they allowed excessive access to the apartment and failed to provide adequate security. However, Judge Sandra Arroyo Salgado, Nisman’s former wife, previously stated in writing that the scene had not been compromised and proposed further investigation into the blood spatter patterns. Her team, including forensic expert Osvaldo Raffo and former Buenos Aires Chief of Police Daniel Salcedo, ultimately concluded that Nisman had died by suicide – a finding that contrasted with the initial narrative pushed by some political factions.
Despite the lack of evidence supporting a homicide, prosecutor Taiano has continued to pursue leads involving intelligence agents, with limited success. He is now reportedly turning his attention to the Army’s intelligence sector, seeking potential connections to former head César Milani.
The case has been plagued by accusations of political interference. Sources indicate that Fein faced pressure to step away from the investigation due to her consistent assertion that “I have no element that tells me that Alberto Nisman was the victim of a homicide.” The previous administration, under Mauricio Macri, allegedly leveraged the Nisman case against its political opponents, and that pattern appears to be continuing.
As one observer noted, the current developments “look like a joke.” After nearly eleven years, the re-emergence of a long-standing imputation, seemingly unrelated to the circumstances of Nisman’s death, coincides with a period of intense scrutiny surrounding the Spagnuolo audio recordings. The timing suggests a deliberate attempt to shift the narrative, highlighting the enduring legacy of the Nisman case as a tool for political maneuvering in Argentina.
